2027-03-21.title: Palm Sunday of the Passion of the Lord
readings: Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord!
I did not hide my face from insult and spitting; I know that I shall not be put to shame
My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
He humbled himself; therefore God also highly exalted him
The Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ according to Mark
2027-03-21.alt: Year B. Holy Week begins. The Lord's entrance into Jerusalem is commemorated in one of three forms given in the Roman Missal: the procession, the solemn entrance or the simple entrance. No Gloria; the Creed is said. The Passion is proclaimed without candles or incense, without the greeting and the signing of the book; all kneel for a short pause after the death of the Lord. Liturgical colour: red.
2027-03-21.verse: he humbled himself and became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross.
theo: Palm Sunday has two faces, and the liturgy shows both. It begins with a joyful procession and ends in the silence of the tomb. Here is how the day unfolds, step by step, so that a family can follow it. 1. Gathering outside. Where possible, the people assemble outside the church, in another church, a hall or the parish grounds, holding branches; in Kerala these are usually tender coconut fronds, kuruthola, often woven into crosses and flowers. The priest and ministers wear red. 2. The opening acclamation. All sing “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel. Hosanna in the highest.” 3. Greeting and blessing. The priest greets the people, briefly invites them to accompany the Lord as he enters his city to accomplish his Passion and Resurrection, blesses the branches with a prayer and sprinkles them with holy water in silence. 4. The Gospel of the entrance. A deacon or the priest proclaims Mark 11:1–10 (or John 12:12–16): the two disciples, the colt never ridden, the cloaks and leafy branches, and the cry “Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord!” 5. The procession. After the invitation “let us go forth in peace,” the procession moves to the church: the thurible, the cross adorned with branches, candles, the Book of the Gospels, the clergy and then all the people with their palms, singing Psalm 24 and Psalm 47 and the ancient hymn “All glory, laud and honour to you, Redeemer King.” 6. Entering the church. As the procession enters, a responsory recalls the children of the Hebrews who went out to meet the Lord. The priest venerates the altar, goes to the chair and, omitting the usual introductory rites, says the Collect. Where a procession outside is not possible, the Missal provides a solemn entrance, with the blessing of branches near the church door or inside, or a simple entrance with the entrance antiphon.

Then the mood changes. The first reading is the third song of the Servant of the Lord: “I gave my back to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who pulled out the beard; I did not hide my face from insult and spitting.” Yet the Servant is not crushed: “The Lord GOD helps me… therefore I have set my face like flint.” The Psalm is the one Jesus himself prayed on the cross: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” It describes with uncanny precision the mocking, the pierced hands and feet, the garments divided by lot, and then turns at the end into praise: “I will tell of your name to my brothers and sisters.” St Paul's hymn in Philippians gives the whole mystery in a few lines: Christ, “though he was in the form of God,” emptied himself, took the form of a slave, “humbled himself and became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him,” so that every knee should bend and every tongue confess “that Jesus Christ is Lord.” The procession of palms and the road to the cross are one movement: the King enters his city in order to give his life.

This year the Passion is read according to St Mark, the oldest and most stark of the four. It begins in Bethany, where an unnamed woman breaks an alabaster jar and pours costly nard on Jesus' head; he says she has anointed his body for burial and “what she has done will be told in remembrance of her.” At the Last Supper he takes bread, blesses, breaks and says, “Take; this is my body,” and over the cup, “This is my blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many.” In Gethsemane he prays, “Abba, Father, for you all things are possible; remove this cup from me; yet, not what I want, but what you want,” while his friends sleep. He is betrayed with a kiss; “All of them deserted him and fled,” even a young man who runs away leaving his linen cloth behind. Before the high priest he is silent until asked whether he is the Messiah: then he answers plainly, “I am.” Peter denies him three times and weeps. Pilate, knowing Jesus is innocent, hands him over to satisfy the crowd; soldiers mock him with purple and thorns; Simon of Cyrene carries his cross. On the cross he is mocked by all, and at three in the afternoon he cries out the first words of Psalm 22. He breathes his last; the curtain of the Temple is torn in two; and a Roman centurion, a pagan, makes the confession that Mark's whole Gospel has been waiting for: “Truly this man was God's Son!” The women watch from a distance, and Joseph of Arimathea lays him in a tomb cut from the rock.

How the Passion is proclaimed. It is read without candles and incense, without the usual greeting, “The Lord be with you,” and without signing the book, because the Lord is going to his death. Often three readers share it: a narrator, a reader for the other voices, and the priest for the words of Christ, while the whole assembly speaks the words of the crowd. When we say “Crucify him!” we confess that it is our sins that crucified him; the Church teaches that the Passion cannot be blamed on all the Jews of that time or on the Jewish people today, and that all sinners were the authors of his suffering (Catechism 597–598; Nostra Aetate 4). At the words “he breathed his last,” everyone kneels in silence for a moment. After a brief homily the Mass continues as usual. Take your blessed palm home and place it behind the crucifix or the family's holy pictures; next year it will be returned to be burned for the ashes of Ash Wednesday. Then keep this week holy: the Chrism Mass, when the bishop blesses the holy oils with his priests (often on Holy Thursday morning, in some dioceses earlier in the week); the Mass of the Lord's Supper on Thursday evening; Good Friday, a day of fasting and abstinence; and the great Easter Vigil on Saturday night. Because 25 March falls on Holy Thursday this year, the Solemnity of the Annunciation is transferred to Monday 5 April 2027, after the Octave of Easter.
conn: A Hebrew cry meaning “save, we pray” (Psalm 118:25), which had become a shout of praise. The crowd adds Psalm 118:26: “Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the LORD.”
Zechariah 9:9 foretold a humble king riding on a colt, the foal of a donkey. A colt never ridden was fit for a sacred purpose (compare Numbers 19:2). Jesus comes as a king of peace, not of war.
Spreading cloaks was a sign of royal welcome (2 Kings 9:13). Leafy branches recall the feasts of Tabernacles and the rededication of the Temple (1 Maccabees 13:51; 2 Maccabees 10:7).

The Roman Missal gives three ways to commemorate the Lord's entrance: the procession from another place; the solemn entrance, with the blessing of branches at or inside the church; and the simple entrance, at Masses where neither is possible.
The processional hymn Gloria, laus et honor was written by Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, around the year 820.
Red is the colour of the Passion and of the blood of martyrs; on Palm Sunday it also honours Christ the King entering his city.
Only Mark tells of the young man who ran off leaving his linen cloth (Mark 14:51–52). Many have seen in him a self-portrait of the evangelist, or an image of every disciple who flees.

Mark's Gospel opens with “the beginning of the good news of Jesus Christ, the Son of God” (1:1); the first human being to proclaim him Son of God after his death is a Gentile soldier at the foot of the cross (15:39).
altar: The palms we wave and the Body we receive belong together. The King hailed with Hosanna gives himself on the altar as the one who said: “Take; this is my body.” At every Mass we sing the crowd's words in the Sanctus: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Hosanna in the highest.”

The sacrifice of the cross that we hear today in the Passion is made present at every Mass, not repeated but offered once for all and given to us. Palm Sunday leads us straight to the altar of Holy Thursday and the cross of Good Friday.
outline: Hold up a palm frond and ask: how long does the joy of a welcome last?
The procession and the humble King on a colt.
Point 2 · The Servant who did not turn back
Isaiah 50 and Gethsemane: “not what I want.”
Psalm 22, the cross and the centurion.
A palm behind the crucifix at home, a reminder all year.
live: Come early with your family, carry your palm and sing; then keep it behind the crucifix at home.
At home this week, read Mark's Passion slowly, one section each day.
Plan now to be present on Thursday evening, Good Friday afternoon and at the Easter Vigil.
Spend an hour before the Blessed Sacrament this week, especially at the Altar of Repose on Thursday night.
fathers: Let us run with him as he hastens to his Passion, and imitate those who went out to meet him. Not with garments or lifeless branches, but let us spread ourselves before his feet, clothed in his grace, so that we may receive the Word who comes.
The cross of Christ is the source of every blessing and the cause of every grace. Through it believers receive strength from weakness, glory from shame and life from death.

It was no great thing for the King of eternity to become King of men. He did not come to be king of Israel to demand taxes or to arm soldiers, but to rule minds, to lead believers into the kingdom of heaven.
magis: The messianic entrance of Jesus into Jerusalem, celebrated each year on Palm Sunday.
Responsibility for the death of Jesus: not the Jewish people as a whole, but all sinners are its authors.
The agony in Gethsemane; Christ's death as the unique and definitive sacrifice.
The three forms of commemorating the Lord's entrance and the proclamation of the Passion.
Holy Week begins on Palm Sunday, which joins the royal triumph of Christ and the proclamation of his Passion.
saints: St Turibius of Mogrovejo (23 Mar, not observed this year)

Archbishop of Lima (1538–1606), he walked and rode thousands of kilometres to visit his vast diocese, learned the local languages, defended the indigenous peoples and founded the first seminary in the Americas. His memorial gives way to Holy Week.

22–24 Mar: Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday of Holy Week. 25 Mar: Holy Thursday, Chrism Mass (in many dioceses that morning) and the Evening Mass of the Lord's Supper; the Annunciation is transferred to Monday 5 April. 26 Mar: Good Friday of the Passion of the Lord, fasting and abstinence. 27 Mar: Holy Saturday; the Easter Vigil after nightfall. 28 Mar: Easter Sunday of the Resurrection of the Lord.
2027-03-21.prayer: Almighty ever-living God, who as an example of humility for the human race to follow caused our Saviour to take flesh and submit to the Cross, graciously grant that we may heed his lesson of patient suffering and so merit a share in his Resurrection. Who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Lord Jesus, King of humble peace, we greet you with palms and we follow you to the cross. Do not let our Hosanna turn into Crucify; keep us awake with you in Gethsemane, faithful with the women at the cross, and full of hope beside your tomb, until Easter morning. Amen.

quick: Jesus enters Jerusalem as a humble King on a colt, greeted with Hosanna.
The Servant does not turn back; Christ empties himself and is obedient to death on a cross.
In Mark's Passion, Jesus dies forsaken, and a Roman centurion confesses him as God's Son.
2027-03-21.action: Take your blessed palm home, place it behind the crucifix, and plan to keep the whole Triduum.
2027-03-21.question: Will my Hosanna today last until Good Friday, or will I run away like the disciples?
catechism: Who is responsible for the death of Christ.
kidsaint: A bishop in Peru, far away in South America, more than four hundred years ago. He travelled over mountains and through jungles, often on foot, to meet every family in his huge diocese, and he learned their languages to tell them about Jesus. Lesson: Jesus came to us; we can go to others to bring him.
2027-03-21.special: Palm Sunday of the Passion of the Lord. Blessing of branches and procession; the Passion according to Mark; Holy Week begins.
term: The week from Palm Sunday to Easter, the most sacred of the year. Its heart is the Paschal Triduum: from the Evening Mass of the Lord's Supper on Holy Thursday, through Good Friday and Holy Saturday, to Evening Prayer on Easter Sunday.

family.explain: Jesus rode into Jerusalem on a young donkey. People put their coats and green branches on the road and shouted: Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! They welcomed Jesus like a king. But Jesus was a gentle King who came to give his life for us on the cross.
family.intention: We pray that our family may walk with Jesus all through Holy Week.
family.ask: Ask: “What can each of us do this week to stay close to Jesus: go to church, give up something, help someone?”

illus: In a coastal parish near Thiruvananthapuram, an old fisherman weaves palm crosses every year for the whole church. A boy once asked why he works so hard on something that will dry up in a week. He held up a finished cross and said: the people waved branches on Sunday and shouted Crucify on Friday. I weave slowly so that I remember, every year, which crowd I want to be in.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, humble King, we welcome you with Hosanna. Give us grace to follow you to the cross. Amen.
share: Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord! (Mark 11:9). How do I welcome Jesus into my life?
Not what I want, but what you want (Mark 14:36). Where do I need to pray this prayer?
Truly this man was God's Son! (Mark 15:39). What does the cross reveal to me about Jesus?
pm.resp: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?
interc: For the Church throughout the world, that she may celebrate Holy Week with faith and devotion.
For all who suffer, feel abandoned or are close to despair, that they may find Christ beside them.
For the persecuted and all who carry the cross, like Simon of Cyrene.
For the elect, who will be baptized at the Easter Vigil.
For our group, that we may stay awake with Jesus and not run away.
pm.close: Father, your Son humbled himself even to death on a cross. Give us a share in his Passion and in his Resurrection. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, today we waved palms and sang Hosanna. And a few minutes later we heard ourselves say: Crucify him! Palm Sunday holds both, the joy of the welcome and the sorrow of the cross, because the King who enters Jerusalem is going there to die.

Jesus comes on a colt, as Zechariah foretold: humble and riding on a donkey. Not a war horse, not an army. The crowd cries: Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord! (Mark 11:9). Hosanna means save us. He will save us, but not in the way they expected.

Isaiah shows us the Servant: I gave my back to those who struck me… I did not hide my face from insult and spitting (Isaiah 50:6). And in Gethsemane Jesus prays: Abba, Father… remove this cup from me; yet, not what I want, but what you want (Mark 14:36). He does not turn back. He freely gives himself for us.

On the cross he cries out: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? (Mark 15:34). He enters into every human loneliness and abandonment. Psalm 22, which begins in that cry, ends in praise. And at that moment a Roman soldier, a foreigner, says what the disciples had not been able to say: truly this man was God's Son! (Mark 15:39).

St Paul sums it up: he humbled himself and became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him (Philippians 2:8–9). The way down is the way up. The cross is the throne of the King.

Take your palm home and put it behind the crucifix. Let it ask you every day: which crowd am I in? Come back on Thursday evening, on Friday afternoon, and on Saturday night for the Easter Vigil. Walk with Jesus to the end, and you will see the morning of the Resurrection. Amen.
kids: Children, today we carried palms like the people in Jerusalem, and shouted Hosanna for Jesus our King! But Jesus was a gentle King, riding on a little donkey.
This week Jesus will die on the cross for us and rise again at Easter. Keep your palm near a cross at home, and say every night: Jesus, I love you, thank you for dying for me.

opts.a: The woman with the alabaster jar
intro: Mark's Passion begins with a woman who breaks a jar of costly ointment over Jesus' head. Jesus says that wherever the Gospel is preached, she will be remembered. Today we remember her.

points.apply: Give Jesus this Holy Week something that costs you.
Spend generous time with the Lord this week in church.

sub: She has done what she could.
points.apply: Attend all three days of the Triduum.

concl: At the start of the Passion, one woman's extravagant love shines out.
Jesus does not ask us to do everything, but to do what we can, with love.
opts.resolve: This Holy Week I will give Jesus something costly: my time, my comfort, my presence at the Triduum.
homily: Dear brothers and sisters, the long Passion we have just heard began quietly, at a dinner in Bethany. While he was at Bethany in the house of Simon the leper, as he sat at the table, a woman came with an alabaster jar of very costly ointment of nard, and she broke open the jar and poured the ointment on his head (Mark 14:3).

She did not pour out a few drops. She broke the jar. That ointment was worth more than three hundred denarii, a year's wages for a labourer. And some of those present grumbled: why was the ointment wasted in this way? (Mark 14:4). They could not understand love that does not calculate. King David once said: I will not offer burnt offerings to the LORD my God that cost me nothing (2 Samuel 24:24). This woman understood that.

Jesus defends her: let her alone; why do you trouble her? She has performed a good service for me (Mark 14:6). Then he says something deeper: she has done what she could; she has anointed my body beforehand for its burial (Mark 14:8). While the disciples still dreamed of a throne, she alone understood that he was going to die. Love sees what cleverness misses.

And immediately after this, Mark tells us that Judas went to the chief priests to betray him. One person breaks a jar for Jesus; another sells Jesus for money. Holy Week puts the choice before us too. Love is strong as death, says the Song of Songs (Song of Songs 8:6). Her love was stronger than the fear and greed around her.

Jesus promised: wherever the good news is proclaimed in the whole world, what she has done will be told in remembrance of her (Mark 14:9). Today we have kept his promise. What will you pour out for Jesus this week? Your time at the Triduum, an hour before the Blessed Sacrament, a reconciliation, a generous gift? Do what you can, and do it with love. Amen.

opts.a: Three men on the way of the Passion
intro: In Mark's Passion three men stand out: Peter who denied and wept, Simon of Cyrene who carried the cross, and Joseph of Arimathea who dared to bury the Lord. In each of them we can find ourselves.

sub: Tears that open the way back.
points.apply: Make a good confession before Easter.

sub: His sons known to the Church.
points.apply: Help someone carry a burden this week without being asked.

sub: A respected man of the council.
points.apply: Speak up for your faith in one place where you usually keep silent.

concl: The Passion is not only a story about Jesus; it is a mirror for us.
We can deny, we can carry, we can dare; and the Lord can use every return.
opts.resolve: This Holy Week I will weep for my sins like Peter, carry another's burden like Simon, and dare like Joseph.
homily: Dear friends, the Passion according to Mark is full of people. Today let us look at three men who meet Jesus on his way to death. In each of them we may see something of ourselves.

First, Peter. At supper he had said: even though all become deserters, I will not. A few hours later, warming himself by a fire, he swore three times that he did not know Jesus. Then the cock crowed a second time, and he remembered. And he broke down and wept (Mark 14:72). Peter's tears were the beginning of his return. A broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise (Psalm 51:17). Holy Week is the time for our tears and our confession.

Second, Simon of Cyrene. They compelled a passer-by, who was coming in from the country, to carry his cross; it was Simon of Cyrene, the father of Alexander and Rufus (Mark 15:21). He did not volunteer. He was forced. But Mark names his sons, which suggests that the family later became known in the Church. The man who was made to carry the cross came to love the One who carried our sins. Surely he has borne our infirmities and carried our diseases (Isaiah 53:4).

Third, Joseph of Arimathea. When all the disciples had fled, this respected member of the council, who was also himself waiting expectantly for the kingdom of God, went boldly to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus (Mark 15:43). It was dangerous to be linked with a crucified man. Joseph risked his name and his place. He wrapped the body in linen and laid it in a tomb, as Isaiah had foretold: they made his grave with the wicked and his tomb with the rich (Isaiah 53:9).

Which of these men am I this week? Perhaps I have denied the Lord by silence or sin: then let me weep like Peter and come back. Perhaps a cross has been laid on me without my choice: then let me carry it with Jesus like Simon. Perhaps I have been a secret disciple: then let me be bold like Joseph. Walk with the Lord through these holy days, and come to the Mass of Easter a changed person. Amen.

intro: Theme: “Truly this man was God's Son!”
The humble King, the Servant who did not turn back, the cry of the forsaken Son, and the name above every name.

q: Rejoice greatly, O daughter Zion! Shout aloud, O daughter Jerusalem! Lo, your king comes to you; triumphant and victorious is he, humble and riding on a donkey, on a colt, the foal of a donkey.

Then those who went ahead and those who followed were shouting, “Hosanna! Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord! Blessed is the coming kingdom of our ancestor David! Hosanna in the highest heaven!”
points.apply: Carry your palm with faith today, and welcome Jesus as King of your home.

points.h: The Servant who did not turn back
q: I gave my back to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who pulled out the beard; I did not hide my face from insult and spitting.
He said, “Abba, Father, for you all things are possible; remove this cup from me; yet, not what I want, but what you want.”
points.apply: Pray the prayer of Gethsemane each night of Holy Week over the hardest thing in your life.

q: My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from helping me, from the words of my groaning?
Now when the centurion, who stood facing him, saw that in this way he breathed his last, he said, “Truly this man was God's Son!”
points.apply: Kneel before the crucifix on Good Friday and make the centurion's confession your own.

q: By myself I have sworn, from my mouth has gone forth in righteousness a word that shall not return: “To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear.”
he humbled himself and became obedient to the point of death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name,
points.apply: Bow your head at the name of Jesus each time you hear it this week.

concl: The King hailed with palms enters Jerusalem to give his life.
Through the cross, the forsaken Son is revealed and exalted, and every knee shall bend.
2027-03-21.resolve: Keep the whole of Holy Week: the Lord's Supper, the Passion and the Easter Vigil.
